Status: working draft for the revised porposal "Publishing WASH Data Together: A Hands-On Retreat for an Open, AI-Ready Sector." Due by Friday 2026-09-04. All five workshop days, the selection process, the funding for participant support, and the timeline before and after the week are drafted. Items marked "to confirm" are settled with the Steering Group. Comments on this draft are welcome for further refinement in a potential preparatory day in October

## Why this week for WASH

What better, open data enables for WASH itself, the strategic question raised in follow-up email from the topic selection session:

- The WHO/UNICEF JMP has not been able to collect data on faecal sludge treatment in the global south for fifteen years. Utilities that manage and share their data would enable regional, national, and global estimates.
- Reuse and combination come before collecting new data.
  - Finding what someone else measured in another place, combining data sources, and re-analysing data that was only ever shared in summary form.
- Data is collected twice today, and evidence disappears with a defunded programme.
  - Monitoring data leaves with the programme, local institutions cannot build on what was measured in their own country, and the next programme starts its baseline from zero.
  - Open and discoverable publication keeps the evidence where the work continues.
- Very little impact monitoring exists.
  - The impact of WASH programmes and WASH research on access to and use of services cannot be measured without shared data as a shared ground truth.
- Closed data makes WASH invisible to AI.
  - Practitioners ask AI tools first and those tools draw only on what is open and machine readable. If WASH evidence sits in closed PDFs, DOCX and other proprietary files, the answers that AI tools produce will remain poor.
- AGUASAN supplies the trust while we provide a shared infrastructure.
  - A 40-year old (fact-check) community across government, NGOs, research, consulting, and networks gains a shared working infrastructure in addition to the knowledge sharing platform (aguasan.ch). The week gives that network a shared GitHub organisation, published packages, and common formats (tidy CSV, data dictionaries) that make one organisation's data combinable with another's, in addition to allowing for increased collaboration through GitHub.
- The 2026 AGUASAN members list consists of about two thirds research, NGO, and consulting, with a small donor and policy group. The hands-on practical workshop speaks to that group as an opportunity to increase their competencies and skills.
- The demand is real
  - The accompanying document "Who signs up for openwashdata training" shows 421 registrations across two course cohorts from 45 countries, most from the global south, most arriving as beginners, and nearly all using AI tools for words rather than for their data (status 2025).

## Working assumptions

- Event week: Monday 6 to Friday 10 September 2027 (beginning of September; exact week to confirm with the organizers).
- 48 participants, working in eight groups of six.
- One dedicated support person per group, so eight supporters in the room during active workshop time. Lars Schöbitz, Elizabeth Tilley, Adriana Clavijo, Emmanuel Mhango (BASEflow NGO, Malawi, to be confirmed). Four more to identify.
- Each group meets online before the workshop, so exchange and a group feeling start early.
- Nobody works alone: everyone keeps their own dataset and outputs, and the group reads each other's code and outputs.
- Venue scouting starts immediately.

## Participant selection

- An application consists of a dataset, a survey, and a one-minute video.
- The dataset is screened at submission. Participants contribute their dataset as scientific content to the week and are invited to co-author the research article on the workshop.
- Cap: 48 participants.
- The survey asks which data collection tools produced the dataset, so the week knows the tools in use and where targeted support is needed (partly covers Chris Zurbrügg's proposal).
- Grant need is declared in a separate field that the quality pass does not see; it counts neither for nor against selection.
- Selection concludes mid-June 2027.
- Selection works in two passes. First a quality pass on the application: the dataset is real and can be brought, the survey answers indicate the applicant will do the pre-work, and the one-minute video shows they can explain why the data matters. Then a diversity pass across everyone who clears the quality bar, to compose a balanced cohort.
- Diversity dimensions balanced in the second pass:
  - Gender: a balanced cohort of women and men.
  - Geography: a strong majority from resource-constrained countries.
  - Seniority: a mix from early-career practitioners to senior staff, so peers learn across levels.
  - Sector: water, sanitation, hygiene, and solid waste management represented, generally open when related to the overall work of these sectors.
  - Employment: academia and research institutes, government and utilities, NGOs and civil society, private sector and consultants, bilateral and philanthropic donors, and multilateral organisations (UN agencies, development banks) represented. All are welcome, but a good balance represesting AGUASAN community is intended.
- The pre-course survey used for "Data Science for openwashdata" (see References)
  - The same instrument behind the demand evidence, is reused here to screen and baseline applicants, so selection rests on data rather than impressions.

## Travel grants

- Travel grants make the diversity goals possible as without them the geography and gender balance above cannot hold.
  -  The people we most want in the room are the least able to self-fund.
- Grants for women from resource-constrained countries, covering travel and accommodation for the workshop week.
- Childcare support, so a parent can bring a child and an additional carer and still take part.
- Funding, two lines stacked:
  - A participant support line in the SDC workshop budget. The request goes to Skat and SDC in the autumn budget clarification.
  - An SNSF Scientific Exchanges application by spring 2027. A member of the ETH Zurich group applies, on a rolling basis 4 to 18 months before the event. The scheme pays travel including visas, accommodation, and meals for participants from abroad, allows practitioners as invitees, and pays a childcare allowance of CHF 200 per accompanying child per night plus the child's travel. Cap CHF 25,000 (roughly 8 to 12 funded participants from abroad), events of at most five days, invitees contribute scientific content. The current guidelines expire 2026-12-31, so the terms are re-checked before applying.
  - Childcare is a named budget line in the workshop budget. EMBO earmarks a fixed childcare sum per funded workshop; the same model applies here.
- The grant count follows the budget answer: the SNSF application covers the first 8 to 12 participants from abroad, the SDC line covers the rest.

## Data collection tools (integrating the withdrawn proposal)

- Every shared dataset shows how it was collected. The application survey asks which data collection tools produced the dataset, which gives a picture of what is in use across the cohort and where gaps exist relative to the tools the digital tools proposal put forward.
- Targeted support follows in the precourse window: participants whose data calls for it get support with the relevant collection tool, rather than presentations to everyone.
- The difference to the workshop's own tools: data management workflows (Git, GitHub, Quarto, data packages) apply to any data; collection tools are specific to a data type, so that support is targeted.

## Retreat elements (daily rhythm)

- Moments for conversation and connection and time in nature are scheduled as an integral part of the week.
- Optional morning run before breakfast (self-organized, a posted route).
- A daily walk: at least one conversation block per day happens walking, for example the case-study debrief or a use-case discussion as a walk-and-talk.
- Being in nature: breaks go outside by default when weather allows.
- Evenings stay deliberately unprogrammed with offers for connection: shared dinner, a fire or lounge space available, at most one light element (for example an open demo corner), no mandatory content.
- The 16:30 close exists to protect the evening and allow for personal time before a potential reconnection in the evening.

## The week

- Ground rules for every day
  - The day starts at 08:30 with the official session start at 09:00 (Monday's arrival buffer and opening are the exception); breaks on the hour (5 and 15 minutes, including small small physical activity exercises); no module ever longer than one hour; close at 16:30 (Friday closes at 15:00).
- Teaching method
  - Every session is a mix of introductory slides, participatory live coding, peer-to-peer instruction, and spaced practice. The training sessions contain no talks. Taught sessions alternate with independent work sessions in which participants work on their own projects.
- Pedagogy
  - The week invests into demonstrating the end product first, so participants see what the it looks like and what it does for the sector and for them personally. The Thursday data management strategy work then reaches back to collection, storage, and management inside their organisation.
- Data security is taught where the risk sits
  - Inside the Tuesday FAIR block (sharing decisions) and inside the Wednesday agentic AI block (what leaves the machine). Both use hands-on examples and end with guardrail measures. The precourse dataset review makes sure no sensitive data enters the workshop in the first place.
- Case studies keep the practical path (aspirational)
  - Their content is developed together with the selected case-study presenters so each one is a worked, hands-on session rather than a talk with slides.
- The Git and GitHub foundations are taught as concepts, but participants apply each one to their own data inside the exercises, so they build the week's output while learning the concepts.

- Responsible sharing
  - The mantra "as open as possible, as closed as necessary" is a trainable structure. Graded sharing (who gets access, crossed with how processed the data is); where data is too sensitive to publish, the cleaning and anonymising code stays open so the process is transparent. There is a defensible way to share something from every dataset.
- Qualitative data floor
  - Voice is biometric data, anonymisation has limits, consent is a process.
- Tidy data discipline
  - One observation per row, one variable per column, no merged cells, no colour as information. The biggest gap between a practitioner's spreadsheet and a publishable dataset.
- The data dictionary that makes data both FAIR and AI-ready
  - Write down what you know about the data, and the same documentation serves a colleague, a successor, and an AI agent.

## Participant outputs

Every participant leaves with:

- Their dataset published as a documented data package (final state by Friday, DOI archiving supported if not already completed).
- Contributor credit: the data package lists every contributor with an ORCID iD, including surveyors, lab managers, and field teams that author lists on scientific articles typically omit, citable through the DOI.
- Durable skills: Git, GitHub, Quarto, FAIR data handling, safe work with agentic AI.
- Named competencies: the skills map onto the Digital Competencies areas information and data literacy, digital content creation, and safety. Tidy data, documentation, and credential and account hygiene are taught as competencies in their own right.
- A personal website, published on Friday.
- A draft plan for their own organisation: a data management strategy outline or data management plan, drafted in the Thursday afternoon work session so the practice transfers home.
- The enrollment path into "Data Science for openwashdata 003"

## Workshop outputs

Beyond the participant level, the week produces:

- 48 published data packages on a shared GitHub organisation, archived with DOIs.
- A concise workshop report by the custodians in the format AGUASAN requests.
- A public interactive website or dashboard that lets others explore the workshop outputs.
- A report with recommendations for the strategic directions of AGUASAN, and in particular SDC, RésEAU, and the Swiss Water Partnership, on data management and open data in the sector.
- Data and results of the registration survey (the ds4owd pre-course survey), anonymised, as a baseline of digital skills in the sector.
- Results of the evaluation survey conducted on the final day.
- Proposed: an impact monitoring plan that tracks the downstream effects of the week on data management practices, at six and twelve months.
- Proposed: a research article on the workshop itself, the week documented as an open data publishing experiment across the sector (who came, the method, the published packages, what the monitoring finds), with custodians and participants as co-authors.

## Post-workshop follow-up

- The follow-up is immediate: ds4owd-003 (TODO: be consistent and use the full wording throughout) starts within two weeks of the workshop week.
- Workshop participants enter the course with their dataset already published and practice their newly developed R skills directly on their own data.
- Exercises are individualized, produced from each participant's data package rather than generic teaching data.
- The evaluation survey results and the custodian report follow within two months of the week; the recommendations report is drafted with the Steering Group.
- The impact monitoring plan runs at six and twelve months, and the research article follows the twelve month point (both proposed).
